scenario.prompt_to_agent:
After an admin added a "temporary backup route" on router0,
IT and CS users report Server Room (1.0.0.x) is unreachable
but Internet Lab (128.168.0.x) works fine. Both used to work.
Diagnose.

injection.action: add a black-hole static for the Server Room prefix

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: router0 routing table — static route to
  1.0.0.0/8 via 127.0.0.1
Mechanism: Linux prefers static routes over RIP-learned routes
  (admin distance / route metric). The new static for 1.0.0.0/8
  points at the loopback, which silently drops the packets.
  128.168.0.0/16 still uses the RIP-learned route via 10.10.0.2.
Localization: router0
Root cause: incorrect static route `1.0.0.0/8 via 127.0.0.1`
Fix: `ip route del 1.0.0.0/8 via 127.0.0.1` (RIP-learned
  route reinstalls automatically)
scenario.fix_spec:
`ip route del 1.0.0.0/8 via 127.0.0.1` (RIP-learned
  route reinstalls automatically)

agent.diagnosis_text:
An admin manually injected a kernel-level static route on router0 outside of FRR,
using `ip route add 1.0.0.0/8 via 127.0.0.1 dev lo`. This route points all traffic
destined for the entire 1.0.0.0/8 block — which covers the Server Room subnet
(1.0.0.x) — toward the loopback interface (127.0.0.1). Because kernel static routes
carry an administrative distance of 0, this route wins unconditionally over the
legitimately learned RIP route for the same prefix (RIP AD=120, next-hop 10.10.0.2
via eth2 toward router1→router2). As a result, router0 immediately discards any
packet arriving from IT or CS hosts that is destined for 1.0.0.x, generating a "TTL
exceeded" ICMP back to the source (confirmed: ICMP unreachables sourced from
192.168.1.1, 100% loss to 1.0.0.5). The Internet Lab (128.168.0.0/16) is
unaffected because no spurious kernel route overlaps that prefix, so RIP correctly
forwards that traffic through router1 to router2 (confirmed: 0% loss to 128.168.0.2).
The FRR running configuration contains no static route — the injected route lives
only in the kernel FIB and is invisible to FRR's configuration files, explaining
why it survives FRR restarts and is easy to overlook.

Root cause: A stray `ip route add 1.0.0.0/8 via 127.0.0.1` kernel static route on
router0 blackholes all Server Room traffic by outcompeting the correct RIP-learned
route.

Corrective fix: On router0, run `ip route del 1.0.0.0/8 via 127.0.0.1` to remove
the bogus static route. The RIP-learned route (via 10.10.0.2) will immediately
become the active FIB entry and restore reachability to the Server Room.

per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly names router0 as the affected device in the diagnosis.
The report explicitly identifies a kernel-level static route in router0's routing table (1.0.0.0/8 via 127.0.0.1) as the root cause.
The report clearly explains that a kernel static route to 127.0.0.1 wins over the RIP-learned route (lower admin distance) and thus directs/absorbs traffic into the loopback, causing the blackhole.
The agent correctly recommends deleting the stray kernel static route (ip route del 1.0.0.0/8 via 127.0.0.1) so the RIP-learned route will become the active FIB entry.

The agent's log contains the key observations (kernel route to 1.0.0.0/8 via 127.0.0.1, RIP-learned route via 10.10.0.2, ping failures sourced from router0, and FRR running-config check), and the writeup's inferences follow logically from those observations with no critical gaps.
